question.text: The Hay-Bunau-Varilla Treaty began construction of this waterway, which connects the Pacific and Atlantic Ocean through its namesake country.
question.clue: The building of this structure was made possible by Walter Reed's work controlling Yellow Fever.

swap.leadin: This policy was enforced by the Volstead Act.
swap.text: Name this policy, which banned the sale or prodution of alcoholic beverages in the United States between 1920 and 1933.
swap.clue: A hatchet was used in activism for this policy by Carrie Nation.

question.text: Scopes was defended by this famous lawyer, who also saved Leopold and Loeb from the death penalty and secured the acquittal of Big Bill Haywood.
question.clue: This man, who severed ties with a railroad company to represent Eugene V. Debs, argued that two University of Chicago students were suggestible to influence byNietzsche and had them plea guilty for killing Bobby Franks.

swap.leadin: In 1914, Woodrow Wilson ordered this man to lead the expedition to capture Pancho Villa.
swap.text: Name this General of the Armies, nicknamed "Blackjack."
swap.clue: This American general was ordered by President Wilson to find Villa following the raid. He was recalled shortly thereafter and was appointed the leader of the American Expeditionary Force in World War I.

question.text: This political party nominated Henry Wallace and Robert LaFollete as its candidates for President.
question.clue: Perhaps the greatest electoral successes of a party by this name came earlier, in California, where Hiram Johnson was elected governor and then Senator on its banner.

swap.leadin: This man paid his way through Hampton Institute by working as a janitor.
swap.text: Name this civil rights leader of the early 20th century and first president of the Tuskegee Institute. This man advocated for gradual social change in contrast to W.E.B. Du Bois.
swap.clue: The most famous student of Sam C. Armstrong, this founder of the National Negro Business League urged everyone to "Cast down your bucket where you are" in a speech.

question.leadin: Identify the following about a period of American history.
question.text: This act, named after a Minnesota Representative, served as the enabling legislation for the 18th amendment. It defined regulations for the commerce of alcohol and its usage in scientific studies.
question.clue: It was sponsored by the chair of the House Judiciary Committee, a congressman from Minnesota, and it gave power of enforcement to the Commissioner of Internal Revenue.

swap.leadin: The losing side of this battle was led by Arsenio Pombo.
swap.text: Identify this battle of the Spanish-American War in which American soldiers gained the high ground on a Cuban hill.
swap.clue: Samuel Sumner commanded the cavalry since "Fighting Joe" Wheeler was deathly ill, but Wheeler rose from his sickbed to meet up with Jacob Kent, who had been dispatched by William Rufus Shafter.

question.text: The Boone and Crockett Club was established by this future US President. The Smithsonian sponsored his expedition to Africa after he left the presidency to his successor William Howard Taft.
question.clue: This president summarized his foreign policy, "Speak softly and carry a big stick."

swap.leadin: This man established a "summer White House" at the State Game Lodge in South Dakota.
swap.text: Identify this tight-lipped president who took office following the death of his predecessor, Warren G. Harding.
swap.clue: He clashed with the American Federation of Labor to put down the Boston Police Strike.

question.leadin: The nomination of one candidate in this election was affirmed in the "smoke-filled room" and supported by his campaign organizer Harry Daugherty.
question.text: Name this election in which Warren Harding's promises of a "Return to Normalcy" earned him a landslide victory.
question.clue: At the Blackstone Hotel in Chicago, a nomination during this election was decided in a "smoke-filled room" by Harry Daugherty.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about American "muckraking" authors.
swap.text: Writer Edwin Markham helped expose this practice, which was restricted by the Keating-Owen Act, an act ruled unconstitutional in the case Hammer v. Dagenhart. This practice was protested in a 1903 march organized by Mother Jones.
swap.clue: The Reverend Alexander McKelway vocally advocated for a law regarding this practice that was later shot down in Hammer v. Dagenhart.

question.text: The greatest project of the Sui dynasty was a project of this type designed to connect northern and southern China by water. Jimmy Carter signed over a US-owned project of this type to Omar Torrijos in 1979.
question.clue: Yellow fever afflicted workers who built one of these structures across the Isthmus of Darien.

swap.leadin: Apologies to our American friends, but, answer some questions about hypocrisy in American history.
swap.text: This event of 1919 killed 21 and injured 150 people, more than four times as many fatalities as the Boston massacre in the same city.
swap.answerHtml: The Great Molasses Flood (accept Boston Molasses Flood, accept Molasses Disaster)
swap.clue: This event, a non-water flood with waves over 9 feet high that caused the city it occurred in to smell of the substance for decades after on hot days.

question.leadin: As attorney general this man brought an anti-trust suit against Northern Securities and won even though that firm didn't compete with itself, but it made it look like Teddy Roosevelt was a trust buster anyway.
question.text: Name this man and attorney general for Teddy Roosevelt, nicknamed "Sleepy Phil," who partially names the bill that ended American involvement in World War I.
question.clue: This attorney for Carnegie Steel was later appointed a Senator by Governor Samuel Pennypacker. As Secretary of State under William Howard Taft, he advocated the system of "dollar diplomacy" in Latin America.

swap.text: This congressman used the data of the 1890 census to set the quotas for new immigrants in the Immigrant Act of 1924, which he co-sponsored and names with Senator David Reed.
swap.clue: This native Kentuckian served as aide-de-camp to Sam Houston during the war of independence, and then was named Texas's Secretary of War by Mirabeau Lamar. The leader of Confederate forces in the West, he was killed at the battle of Shiloh.

question.text: The alleged mastermind behind the fix was this Jewish mobster and bootlegger who mentored Lucky Luciano and was killed in New York City in 1928 over poker debts.
question.clue: This Jewish-American mobster known as the "Brain." He helped fix the 1919 World Series, was the inspiration for Meyer Wolfsheim in The Great Gatsby, and may have been killed by Dutch Schultz.

swap.leadin: Name these things about the Panic of 1907.
swap.text: The next element of the panic was a run on this trust company after it fired its president, Charles Barney. It shares its name with the fictional persona Diedrich, which Washington Irving used to write A History of New York.

question.leadin: Answer the following about American pietism around the turn of the 20th century, FTPE.
question.text: This pastor of the Central Congregational Church in Topeka and leader of the Social Gospel is best known for his sermon stories which were novelized as the popular book In His Steps.

swap.text: A key member of Taylor's society was this woman who set up the National Consumer's League and was a resident of Hull House with Jane Addams and Grace Abbott. This author of Modern Industry in Relation to the Family is best remembered for opposing child labor.
